Highly Regioselective and Helix-Sense Selective Living
Polymerization of Phenyl and Alkoxyallene Using Chiral Nickel(II)
Catalysts
Li Zhou, § Chong-Long Li, § Run-Tan Gao, Shu-Ming Kang, Lei Xu, Xun-Hui Xu, Na Liu, *
and Zong-Quan Wu *
Cite This: Macromolecules 2021, 54, 679 −686 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Facile synthesis of high optically active helical polymers from
achiral monomers still remains a great challenge. In this work, two chiral Ni(II)
catalysts bearing chiral R- or S-2a ligands were facilely prepared which can
eﬃciently initiate the living/controlled polymerization of allene monomers and
aﬀord well-de ﬁned polyallenes in high yields with controlled molecular masses
(Mns) and low molecular mass distributions ( Mw/Mns). The catalysts showed
interesting regioselectivity on the cumulated double bonds of allene monomers,
as the polymerizations were highly selective which occurred on 2,3-double
bonds. Moreover, the polymerization of achiral allene monomers using chiral Ni(II) catalysts showed remarkable helix-sense
selectivity. The yielded polyallenes exhibited high optical activity due to the formation of a predominant one-handed helix as
revealed by circular dichroism, UV −vis, and direct atomic force microscopy (AFM) observations as well. The predominant one-
handed helicity of the generated polyallenes was solely determined by the chirality of the Ni(II) catalysts.
■ INTRODUCTION
Helix is one of the most important secondary structural motifs
in biopolymers and also in synthetic macromolecules.
1−3 The
one-handed helical conformation adopted by biological
macromolecules such as protein and DNA plays important
living functions including molecular recognition, catalysis,
inheritance, replication, and so on.
4−6 A slight damage on the
helical structure of biomacromolecules can cause a variety of
severe diseases. For example, misfolding the helix of proteins
into an extended β-sheet may result in amyloid structures
accompanied by grievous dysfunctions including Alzheimer ’s
disease, Parkinson ’s disease, and diabetes.
7,8 Therefore,
stimulated by the biological helices and functions, synthetic
helical polymers have attracted great attention from synthetic
chemistry to materials science and biological engineering.
9−13
These research studies not only explore the structure and
property of the unique helices in nature but also develop new
materials with novel functions.
14−17 Moreover, the study on a
helical polymer can bring out a new structural platform for the
development of novel functional materials.
18−21 Although the
helical polymer is still on the preliminary research stage, it has
exhibited a wide range of applications, such as those in
enantiomer separation, chiral switch, asymmetric catalysis,
circularly polarized luminescence (CPL), and optoelectronic
devices among others.
22−26 From the reported helical
polymers, polyallene is of particular interest because it contains
reactive exo-double bonds along the backbone which can be
further decorated with other intriguing functionalities.
27,28
Polyallene is generally produced through the radical polymer-
ization or coordination polymerization of the corresponding
allene monomers using transition-metal complexes as cata-
lysts.
29,30 The living/controlled coordination polymerization
can yield polyallenes with expected molecular mass and low
polydispersity.31,32 However, both the accumulated double
bonds of allene monomers can be polymerized and result in
polyallene with complex architectures.
33−36 Thus, developing a
new method for living/controlled polymerization of allene
monomers with high regioselectivity of the accumulated
double bonds is greatly desired.
On the other hand, optically active helical polyallenes were
usually prepared from the polymerization of chiral allene
monomers with high enantiomeric purity. 37 The helix-sense
was determined by the chirality of the monomers, and a large
amount of chiral materials was consumed during the
polymerization.
38 As we know, enantiopure materials are
generally limited and expensive except for those derived from
the natural product, which may further limit the type and
scope of the available monomers. Thus, synthesis of large
optically active helical polyallene from achiral materials is
greatly intriguing because a plenty of optically active polymers

can be facilely obtained from a tiny amount of chiral catalysts,
initiators, or additives through chirality transfer and
ampliﬁcation strategies.
39 Moreover, such kind of helical
polymers can exhibit high optical activity derived solely from
one-handed helicity, without containing any other chiral
moieties on the polymer pendants or on the chain ends.
However, helical polyallene prepared from achiral allene
monomers has seldom been reported owing to the limited
polymerization strategy albeit this strategy possessing many
advantages. Thus, exploring a novel catalyst or initiator for
controlled synthesis of optically active helical polymers from a
achiral allene monomer with high region-selectivity is very
interesting.
Herein, we report on a family of chiral nickel(II) catalysts
which can initiate the living polymerization of various allene
monomers with high region and helix-sense selectivity. The
polymerization occurred with high selectivity on the 2,3-
double bond among the two accumulated double bonds of
allenes. Moreover, the polymerization of achiral allene
monomers by the chiral Ni(II) catalysts produced predom-
inantly one-handed helical polyallene with large optical activity
due to the asymmetric induction of the chiral catalysts.
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
First, to screen out an excellent chiral Ni(II) catalyst, a family
of chiral phosphine ligands ( 2a−2f) were designed and
synthesized ( Scheme 1 ). After full characterization, these
ligands were treated with ( π-allyl)NiOCOCF
3 in toluene at
room temperature to produce the desired Ni(II) catalysts. 40,41
The ratio of the ligand to Ni(II) was tentatively ﬁxed at 1/1.
The resulting catalyst solutions were directly used in the
polymerization of allene monomers without further isolation
and puri ﬁcation steps to lower the risk of catalyst
decomposition. Three allene monomers 1a−1c were designed
and synthesized followed the literature with some modi ﬁca-
tions (see Supporting Information for the details of syn-
thesis).
37 The activity of the Ni(II) catalysts was investigated
through the polymerization of allene monomer 1a in CH 2Cl2
at 25 °C( [1a]0/[Ni]0 = 100, [1a]0 = 0.2 M). After most of the
monomer was assumed, the polymerization solution was
precipitated into methanol and the yielded polymers were
collected via ﬁltration. The isolated polymers were ﬁrst
analyzed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), and the
results were summarized in Table 1 . It was found that all the
Ni(II) catalysts can promote the polymerization of monomer
1a, and polymers with similar molecular mass ( M
n = ca. 40
kDa) and low polydispersity ( Mw/Mn < 1.28) were a ﬀorded.
However, the catalysts with di ﬀerent ligands also showed
diﬀerent behaviors on the polymerizations. The ligand R-2a
showed highest activity among others because it took a short
polymerization time (ca. 15 h) and gave the expected polymer
in high yield with expected M
n and quite low dispersity with
Mw/Mn = 1.05 (run 1, Table 1 ). The Ni(II) catalysts bearing
R-2c and S-2e ligands showed a lower activity as the
polymerization took more than three days even at higher
temperatures, and the yields were low (run 3 and run 5 in
Table 1 ; Figure S18 in Supporting Information ). Thus, the
Ni(II) catalyst bearing the R-2a ligand was the good catalyst
for the polymerization of allene monomer 1a. The in ﬂuence of
the ratio of the R-2a ligand to Ni(II) was also investigated. It
was found that the best ratio of R-2a to Ni(II) was 1/1; an
increase or decrease of the ratio would broaden the molecular

The behaviors of the polymerizations initiated by Ni(II)/ R-
2a were studied in more detail. A couple of polymerizations of
1a initiated by Ni(II)/ R-2a were parallelly carried out in
CH2Cl2 at room temperature but under di ﬀerent molar ratios
of the monomer to the Ni(II) catalyst ([ 1a]0/[Ni]0). All the
polymerizations a ﬀorded the expected polymers in high yields
(>85%) with unimodal and symmetrical SEC traces ( Figure
1a). The elution peaks moved to a low retention-time region
with an increased [ 1a]0/[Ni]0 ratio. The Mn of the generated
polymers showed a linear correlation to the initial ratio of
[1a]
0/[Ni]0, and all the isolated polymers had low dispersity
with Mw/Mn < 1.08 ( Figure 1 b; run 1 −8i n Table 2 ). This
result suggests that the polymerization of 1a initiated by
Ni(II)/R-2a proceeded in a chain-growth living/controlled
fashion. SEC tracking experiment of the polymerization further
supported the living fashion of the polymerization ([ 1a]
0 = 0.2
M, [1a]0/[Ni]0 = 50). As displayed in Figure 2, the SEC peak
of the generated polyallene continually moved to a higher Mn-
area and remained monodisperse. The plot of the Mn value
against the monomer conversion revealed that the Mn
increased linearly to the monomer conversion while the Mw/
Mn kept narrow throughout the whole polymerization process
(Figure 3 a). Interestingly, the polymerization was quite fast;
>90% of monomer was consumed within 8 h. Kinetic analysis
demonstrated that the polymerization agreed with the ﬁrst-
order reaction mechanism, and the polymerization rate
constant was 7.8 × 10
−5 s−1 (Figure 3 b). These results clearly
indicated that the Ni(II) catalyst bearing a chiral phosphine
ligand R-2a was an excellent catalyst for the living polymer-
ization of allene monomer 1a. Thus, this initiating system of
Ni(II)/R-2a was further extended to the polymerization of
monomer 1b and 1c under similar experimental conditions to
those of 1a. As expected, the polymerizations proceeded in
living/controlled fashions and gave desired polyallenes in high
yields with tunable M
n and relatively low Mw/Mn (run 11 −14
in Table 2 ; Figure S21 −S22 and Table S2 in Supporting
Information). These studies further veri ﬁed the high catalytic
activity of the Ni(II)/ R-2a catalyst.
The chemical structure of the generated polymers was
investigated by 1H, 31P, and 13C NMR and FT-IR as well. 1H
NMR spectra of monomer 1a and the resulting R-poly-1a100
recorded in CDCl3 are displayed in Figure 4a,b, respectively. In
contrast to the sharp signals of 1a, the resonances of the
resulting polymer were quite broad. The protons of the

terminal double bond (2,3-double bond, a) of the monomer
completely disappeared, indicative of the full polymerization of
the terminal double bonds. Accordingly, a new broad
resonance appeared at 3.02 ppm on the
1H NMR spectrum
of the R-poly-1a100 polymer, derived from the exo-proton of
the polymerized double bond. Interestingly, no peak can be
detected around 5.0 ppm, corresponding to the polymerization
of 1,2-double bonds of 1a.42,43 This result con ﬁrmed that the
polymerization of the allene monomer 1a mainly occurred on
the 2,3-double bonds, suggesting the high regioselectivity of
the polymerization. The unreacted 1,2-double bond of the
monomer was overlapped with the phenyl protons and cannot
be clearly discerned. It is worthy to note that the resonance of
N−H shifted to the down ﬁeld compared to the monomer 1a.
This is reasonable because of the formation of the intra-
molecular hydrogen bonding between the N −H and C Oo f
adjacent repeating units, which further supports the generation
of expected polymer. The existence of intramolecular hydrogen
bonding between the N −H and C O of adjacent repeating
units could also be further con ﬁrmed by the FT-IR spectra of
R-poly-1a
100 measured in toluene and CHCl 3 solution,
respectively (Figure S23 in Supporting Information ). 13C
NMR analyses further veri ﬁed the formation of the expected
polymer. As displayed in Figure 4 d, the resonance of the
carbons of R-poly-1a100 was quite clear; only the 2,3-
polymerized product can be clearly observed, con ﬁrming the
high 2,3-selective polymerization of the catalyst. In order to
ﬁgure out the syn or anti con ﬁguration of the double bond of

the pendant, a series of NMR and FT-IR spectra were
recorded; however, it was hard to determine the syn or anti
conﬁguration of the double bond. Furthermore,
1H, 31P NMR,
IR, and CD spectra were recorded to con ﬁrm whether the
Ni(II)-complex resided on the end chain of the isolated
polyallenes. However, no detectable signals belonging to the
phosphine ligand could be observed, even on the polymers
with very low M
n. Particularly, no signals of the ligand on 31P
NMR could be discerned, con ﬁrming that the Ni(II)-complex
was decomposed from the chain end of the polymer during the
process of precipitation (Figure S24 in Supporting Informa-
tion). Probably, the phosphine ligand was oxidized during the
postpolymerization workup, and the Ni(II)-complex was
decomposed and left from the polymer chain end. The
living/controlled polymerizations of monomer 1b and 1c by
Ni(II)/ R-2a all occurred at the 2,3-double bond as
demonstrated by
1H NMR analyses (Figure S11 and Figure
S14 in Supporting Information ). Collectively, these studies
support the high e ﬃciency and regioselectivity of the catalyst.
Since the polymerization gave an expected well-de ﬁned
polymer with anticipated Mn, narrow Mw/Mn, and high 2,3-
selectivity, the chiroptical properties of the generated polymers
were further investigated. Although monomer 1a was achiral
and circular dichroism (CD) silent, the isolated R-poly-1a100
showed large optical activity as revealed by CD and UV −vis
absorption analyses. The CD and UV −vis spectra of monomer
1a and R-poly-1a100 are displayed in Figure 5 a. Monomer 1a
showed strong absorption with the maximum located at 255
nm. While the resulting R-poly-1a
100 showed absorption at a
relatively longer wavelength region, the absorption band
around 260 nm of R-poly-1a100 may also contribute to the
π−π* transition of the benzene ring. As anticipated, monomer
1a was CD silent while the produced R-poly-1a100 exhibited
distinct CD at the backbone absorption region, indicative of
the predominant one-handed helix adopted by the polymer
backbone. The CD intensity increased with the increase of the
degree of the polymerization (DP) until the Mn reached to
40.2 kDa, suggesting that a stable helix was formed when the
DP reached to ca. 100. The excess of the left-handed helix of
R-poly-1a100 was calculated to be ca. 10% compared to the
single left-handed polyallene reported by our group pre-
viously.
37 This result suggested that a predominated left-
handed helix was selectively produced using R-2a as the ligand
in the polymerization. Although the helix-sense excess of the R-
poly-1a100 was not high, this was one of the few methods to
obtain chiral polyallenes from achiral monomers.
The optical activity of the polymers measured by optical
rotation revealed a similar relationship between the optical
activity with the M
n (Figure 5 b,c). The diluting experiment
demonstrated that the CD and absorption intensities of R-
poly-1a100 decreased linearly with the diluted concentration,
while the g265 was constant. These results indicated that the
helical structure was maintained during the dilution and also
supported that the optical activity comes from the polymer
itself and not the intermolecular self-assembly or aggregation
(Figure S25 in Supporting Information). To further verify that
the optical activity was attributed to the asymmetric induction
of the chiral Ni(II) catalyst, S-poly-1a
100 was prepared under
the same conditions through living and regioselective polymer-
ization of 1a using Ni(II)/S-2a as the catalyst, the enantiomer
of Ni(II)/R-2a. For comparison, CD and UV −vis spectra of S-
poly-1a
100 were recorded and also displayed in Figure 5 a. It
was found that S-poly- 1a100 showed almost the same
absorption behavior to that of R-poly-1a100, suggesting that
the chemical structures of the two polymers were almost the
same. Interestingly, S-poly-1a100 also exhibited an intense CD
at the absorption region of the backbone but was mirror
imaged to that of R-poly-1a
100 due to the opposite handedness
of the helical backbone to that of R-poly-1a100. This result
veriﬁed that the optically active helical backbone of these

polymers indeed comes from the asymmetric induction of the
chiral catalyst during the polymerization. The helical structure
of the generated polymers was quite stable and exhibited
intense CD in various organic solvents, such as tetrahydrofuran
(THF), CH
2Cl2,C H C l 3, and so forth. (Figure S26 in
Supporting Information ). The CD intensity varied with the
polarity of the solvents probably due to the variation on the
hydrogen bonding strength between the adjacent repeating
units in solvents. Accordingly, the g265 value of R-poly-1a100 in
THF decreased from 3.10 × 10−4 to 1.81 × 10−4 when the
temperature of the solution was increased from −25 to 55 °C,
and the g265 value of R-poly-1a100 could be increased to original
intensity upon the solution cooling to −25 °C. which
suggested the dynamic and helix memory characters of the
synthesized helical polyallene ( Figure 5 d and Figure S27 in
Supporting Information ).44 Then, the CD intensity of R-poly-
1a100 was measured in THF and CHCl 3 alternately; it could be
observed that the solvent-dependent CD changes were
reversible too (Figure S28 in Supporting Information ). The
slight CD variations on the temperature and solvents may be
ascribed to the racemization of the helix-sense at higher
temperatures and polar solvents, which also suggested that the
polyallene may have partial dynamic and chiral memory
properties. However, the precise mechanism of the helix-
revision is not very clear under the current stage. The helix-
sense selective manner of the living polymerization initiated by
the Ni(II)/R-2a can be extended to monomer 1b and 1c. The
produced polymers also exhibited intense CD at the backbone
absorption region (Figure S29 in Supporting Information )
because of the formation of one-handed predominant helices
induced by the chiral catalyst. It is worthy to note that the large
optical activities of the synthetic helical polyallene solely come
from the helicity of the main chain because there were no
chiral moieties on the pendants or at the chain ends. The chiral
phosphine ligand was removed during the postpolymerization
workup process. Therefore, it can be concluded that the
chirality economy of the polymerizations using the chiral Ni
(II) catalyst was quite high. That is, the catalytic amount of the
chiral ligand can produce a large amount of chiral materials
with high optical activity.
In order to get more details, helical structures of S-poly-1a
100
and R-poly-1a100 were further convinced by atomic force
microscope (AFM) investigations. The dilute solutions of S-
poly-1a100 and R-poly-1a100 in THF were cast onto highly
oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) and slowly evaporated to
dryness in air. 45−47 Then, AFM observations were performed,
and the recorded images were displayed in Figure 6 a,b. As
expected, right- and left-handed twisted ﬁbers were observed
clearly on the samples of S-poly-1a100 and R-poly-1a100,
respectively. Meanwhile, from the zoomed AFM images, the
helix-sense of each polym er chain could be clearly
distinguished ( Figure 6 c,d). The average height and diameter
of the helical chain of S-poly-1a
100 were estimated to be ca.
2.52 and 2.17 nm, respectively ( Figure 6 a; 6e and Figure S30
in Supporting Information ). The space between neighboring
polymer chains was ca. 3.02 nm, while the helical pitch was ca.
1.88 nm ( Figure 6 g,h). Moreover, the helical array of the
pendants in clockwise direction can be clearly observed at 64 ±
2° relative to the backbone axis from the high-resolution AFM
images. Accordingly, the diameter and helical pitch of R-poly-
1a
100 were ca. 2.10 and 1.89 nm, respectively, while the helical
array of the pendants was anticlockwise with 64 ± 2°, similar
to those of S-poly-1a100, suggesting the formation of stereo-
regular helical polyallenes ( Figure 6 g,h).
Beside CD and AFM analyses, computer simulation of R-
poly-1a100 was carried out to further con ﬁrm the helix of the
main chain. As shown in Figure 6 f,i, the views of the three-
dimensional optimal structure from the top and side are shown
using a 30-mer of R-poly-1a
m as a model. It could be seen that
a3 1 rod-like single-handed helical conformation was formed,
which was the most stable conformation of R-poly-1am. There
were three parts including the aromatic region, the periphery,
and the twisting main chain core in the polymer chain of S-
poly-1a
m (Figure 6 f). This structure could be considered as
columns like the helical polymer with similar structures. The
structure could be regarded similar to a helical polymer having
a similar structure. At last, due to the rigid rod-like feature, R-
poly-1a
100 and S-poly-1a100 exhibited a liquid crystal phase as
revealed by polarized optical micrographs obtained in the
concentrated THF solutions at room temperature (Figure S31
in Supporting Information ).
■ CONCLUSIONS
In summary, we have developed two new kinds of chiral Ni(II)
catalysts, which can initiate a living/controlled polymerization
of various allene monomers and generate expected polymers in
high yields with tunable M
ns and low Mw/Mns. Remarkably,
the polymerizations showed very high regioselectivity, and the

polymerizations mainly occurred on the 2,3-double bond of
the allene monomers. Moreover, the living polymerizations of
achiral allene monomers by chiral Ni(II) catalysts exhibited an
interesting helix-sense selectivity, generating high optically
active helical polyallene with a predominant one-handed helix.
The helicity of the polyallene was con ﬁrmed by CD, UV −vis,
and direct AFM observations. We believe that the present
study provides not only a new method for controlled synthesis
of optically active helical polymers but also a family of
functional materials with great potentials in asymmetric
catalysis, CPL, and so forth.
